problems.form_value: ai_design records: Dunn's post hoc test, Bonferroni corrected: no significant differences 'among all the individual approaches (all p > 0.05)'. Per-arm records: Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post hoc test, Bonferroni corrected: 'all p > 0.05'. statistics_available: figure_only, p_value_only. Reconciliation: 'Its post hoc tests compare pairs, and every pair gave p > 0.05.'
problems.source_says: The paper names Dunn's test once, in its general description of the analysis: 'We performed Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction as post-hoc testing' (p. 8, Section 5). For novelty and usefulness it prints one sentence that covers both the pooled Mann-Whitney comparison and the four-approach comparison. It does not say that Dunn's tests were run for these two outcomes, and it prints no p-value for any pair. The paper also does not say whether it ran pairwise tests after a Kruskal-Wallis result that was not significant. So the statements that Dunn's test gave p > 0.05 and that 'every pair gave p > 0.05' are inferences. For any single pair, the only printed statistic is the shared bound 'all p > 0.05', so p_value_only here means a shared bound, not a pair-specific p-value. Direction no_clear_difference still holds for every pair: Section 6.3 says 'there was not a single setting wherein using LLMs yielded significant benefits for designers relative to not using them' (p. 13). Fix: in each per-arm and arm-vs-arm record, write 'Kruskal-Wallis across the four approaches (the paper names Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction as its post hoc procedure). Only the blanket statement is printed, with no pair-specific test.' Remove 'every pair gave p > 0.05' from the reconciliation note. This is minor. It changes no direction, construct, unit, or eligibility decision.
problems.quote: As Figure 5 shows, there were no statistically significant differences for either, between the manual and the llm-all group but also among all the individual approaches (all p > 0.05).
problems.locator: p. 8, Section 5 (test procedure); pp. 8-9, Section 5.2 (result); p. 13, Section 6.3 and Table 2; full-text search finds Dunn's test only on p. 8

confirmed: Both outcomes are rater scores of participants' frames, not self-reports. Raters assessed 'how novel and useful a perspective each problem frame introduces when compared to the original problem description', and the 15 raters scored frames 'generated by other participants' (p. 7, Section 4.4; p. 8, Section 4.5; p. 6, Figure 4 caption).

AI was available while the rated frames were written. LLM-arm participants were 'free to directly submit frames or build on LLM-generated ones', and FREE-FORM participants used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) and submitted the log. No frame was written after AI was removed, and neither construct is diversity. So question with_ai, ai_available_when_produced yes, and timing immediate follow the codebook rule (p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 7, Section 4.5; codebook section 1).

Constructs novelty and usefulness fit. Each rating judges one frame against the original problem description, with questionnaires 'designed to assess the novelty and utility of ideas [21]'. No measure compares different people's frames, so no diversity construct applies (p. 7, Section 4.4; codebook section 6).

Measure expert_raters has support. The paper calls the raters '15 expert designers', invited because they answered 3 or more quiz items correctly. Table 11 lists 3, 11, and 1 raters with 3, 4, and 5 correct answers and mean design experience of 6.33, 7.86, and 1.00 years. They came from the same Prolific and CloudResearch pool, which the form notes in open_questions (p. 6, Figure 4 caption; p. 8, Section 4.5; p. 25, Table 11).

Unit output and n_units 280 match the paper's own analysis: 'We analyzed the 280 problem frames that participants selected as the best ones from their reframing.' Each person contributes one rated frame, and the power analysis uses n = 280 (p. 8, Section 5 and Section 5.1).

measure_detail facts check out: raters blind to condition, 36 frames per rater (4 approaches x 3 problems x 3 frames), questionnaires from Doshi and Hauser [21], a 1-9 axis in Figure 5, and no stated scale, raters per frame, or rule for combining ratings (p. 5, Section 4.1; p. 6, Section 4.3; p. 7, Section 4.4; p. 8, Figure 5).

Arm sizes in the contrasts match the Figure 8 table on the PDF page: MANUAL 62, DIRECT 72, STRUCTURED 88, FREE-FORM 58, total 280. LLM-ALL 218 matches 'Of the 218 participants in the llm-all group' (p. 9, Figure 8; p. 9, Section 5.2).

The pooled LLM-ALL vs MANUAL record matches the source: Mann-Whitney U test, the verbatim 'all p > 0.05' sentence, Figure 5 left panel for novelty and right panel for usefulness. No means, SDs, or test statistics for either outcome appear anywhere in the paper (p. 8, Section 5 and Figure 5; pp. 8-9, Section 5.2).

Direction no_clear_difference holds for every contrast. Table 2 says 'No increase in novelty or usefulness from the manual to LLM-based approaches', and Section 6.3 says no LLM setting gave a significant benefit (p. 8, Figure 5 caption; p. 13, Table 2 and Section 6.3).
primary paper_primary holds for both outcomes: 'our primary hypothesis was this: H1: Using an LLM during problem reframing increases the novelty and usefulness of the outputs' (p. 4, Section 3.1).
Self-reported measures are correctly left out. Agency and ownership use 'self-assessment items', and CSI and NASA-TLX measure perceived helpfulness and effort (p. 7, Section 4.4; p. 10, Section 5.4).

No outcome that bears on the three questions is missing. A full-text search finds no diversity, similarity, or homogenization measure on the frames, and no frame is written after AI is removed. The expertise analysis (Z = 2.70, p = 0.01; FREE-FORM Z = 2.31, p = 0.06) compares quiz-defined experts with novices inside the LLM arms, not AI with no AI, and the form keeps it in notes. The pilot (N = 36) compares no conditions (pp. 11-12, Section 5.5 and Figure 10; p. 25, Appendix D).

Numbers in the form's notes match: CSI 64.28 (SD 18.90), 64.85 (SD 20.00), 61.01 (SD 17.19); chi2(3, N = 280) = 0.70, p = 0.87; agency Z = 2.05, p = 0.04 and Z = 2.29, p = 0.02 (15.69 percent); experts in the LLM arms 22 + 22 + 17 = 61 (p. 10, Section 5.4; p. 11, Section 5.5; p. 12, Section 5.5; p. 9, Figure 8).
summary: The core coding of c116's two outcomes holds: 15 blind raters scored the novelty and usefulness of each participant's selected frame, written with GPT-4o available in the LLM arms, so question with_ai, the constructs, expert_raters, unit output with 280 frames, the arm sizes, and the 'all p > 0.05' result all match the PDF, and no outcome that bears on the three questions is missing. The conclusion is refuted only on a minor point: the pairwise records credit 'all p > 0.05' to Dunn's post hoc tests, and the reconciliation says 'every pair gave p > 0.05', but the paper names Dunn's test only as its general procedure and prints one blanket sentence for novelty and usefulness, with no pair-specific test.
